title: Perfect pitch and the train-whistle game on the Hines bus
summary: Wilson says he has always played by ear and tells how bandmates quizzed him on notes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When did you start depending on your ear, as opposed to reading?
Well, that came natural. Even when I was taking violin lessons.
Really? That young?
Yeah.
You could play what you heard?
Play what I heard, yeah. Yeah, the minute you hit a note, I knew what it was.
You've got perfect pitch?
Uh-huh.
That's a great gift.
Yeah, we used to play games on the bus.
How do you mean?

One of the guys would ask me -- a train whistle would blow, or different sounds. What note was that Quinn? They called me Quee pee, that was my name, Que-pee. That was my nickname. What note was that, Que-pee?
Was this with the Earl Hines band?
Uh-huh. That's when we were traveling on the bus.
Train whistles always sound like a diminished chord to me.
Yeah. It's like a triad.
And that was --
Especially these diesel horns, you know.
Yeah. Sound like the beginning of "Dipper Mouth Blues,"
Yeah, (laughing).
